L1241:     rule <k> REST || false => REST ... </k>
L1242: 
L1243:     rule <k> REST && true  => REST  ... </k>
L1244:     rule <k> _    && false => false ... </k>
L1245: This will generate rules like this in the case of `_||_` (note that `BE1` will not be heated unless `isKResult(BE2)` is true, meaning that `BE2` must be evaluated first):
L1246: 
L1247:     k
L1248: 
L1249:     rule <k>  BE1:BExp || HOLE:BExp => HOLE ~> BE1 ||  [] ... </k> [heat]
L1250:     rule <k> HOLE:BExp ||  BE2:BExp => HOLE ~>  [] || BE2 ... </k> requires isKResult(BE2) [heat]
L1251: 
L1252:     rule <k> HOLE:BExp ~>  [] || BE2 => HOLE ||  BE2 ... </k> [cool]
L1253:     rule <k> HOLE:BExp ~> BE1 ||  [] =>  BE1 || HOLE ... </k> [cool]
L1254: ### Context Declaration
L1255: 
L1256: Sometimes more advanced evaluation strategies are needed. By default, the `strict` and `seqstrict` attributes are limited in that they cannot describe the context in which heating or cooling should occur. When this type of control over the evaluation strategy is required, `context` sentences can be used to simplify the process of declaring heating and cooling when it would be unnecessarily verbose to write heating and cooling rules directly.
L1257: For example, if the user wants to heat a term if it exists under a `foo` constructor if the term to be heated is of sort `bar`, one might write the following context (with the optional label):
L1258: 
L1259:     k
L1260: 
L1261:     context [foo]: foo(HOLE:Bar)
L1262: 
L1263: Once again, note that `HOLE` is just a variable, but one that has special meaning to the compiler indicating the position in the context that should be heated or cooled.
L1264: 
L1265: This will automatically generate the following sentences:
L1266: 
L1267:     k
L1268:     rule [foo-heat]: <k> foo(HOLE:Bar) => HOLE ~> foo([]) ... </k> [heat]
L1269:     rule [foo-cool]: <k> HOLE:Bar ~> foo([]) => foo(HOLE) ... </k> [cool]
L1270: 
L1271: The user may also write the K cell explicitly in the context declaration if they want to match on another cell as well, for example:
L1272: 
L1273:     k
L1274: 
L1275:     context <k> foo(HOLE:Bar) ... </k> <state> .Map </state>
L1276: 
L1277: This context will now only heat or cool if the `state` cell is empty.
L1278: ### Side conditions in context declarations
L1279: 
L1280: The user is allowed to write a side condition in a context declaration, like so:
L1281: 
L1282:     k
L1283: 
L1284:     context foo(HOLE:Bar) requires baz(HOLE)
L1285: 
L1286: This side condition will be appended verbatim to the heating rule that is generated, however, it will not affect the cooling rule that is generated:
L1287: 
L1288:     k
L1289: 
L1290:     rule <k> foo(HOLE:Bar) => HOLE ~> foo([]) ... </k> requires baz(HOLE) [heat]
L1291:     rule <k> HOLE:Bar ~> foo([]) => foo(HOLE) ... </k> [cool]
L1292: ### Rewrites in context declarations
L1293: 
L1294: The user can also include exactly one rewrite operation in a context declaration if that rule rewrites the variable `HOLE` on the left hand side to a term containing `HOLE` on the right hand side. For exampl;e:
L1295: 
L1296:     k
L1297: 
L1298:     context foo(HOLE:Bar => bar(HOLE))
L1299: 
L1300: In this case, the code generated will be as follows:
L1301: 
L1302:     k
L1303: 
L1304:     rule <k> foo(HOLE:Bar) => bar(HOLE) ~> foo([]) ... </k> [heat]
L1305:     rule <k> bar(HOLE:Bar) ~> foo([]) => foo(HOLE) ... </k> [cool]
L1306: This can be useful if the user wishes to evaluate a term using a different set of rules than normal.
L1307: ### `result` attribute
L1308: 
L1309: Sometimes it is necessary to be able to evaluate a term to a different sort than `KResult`. This is done by means of adding the `result` attribute to a strict production, a context, or an explicit heating or cooling rule:
L1310: 
L1311:     k
L1312: 
L1313:     syntax BExp ::= Bool
L1314:                   | BExp "||" BExp [seqstrict(2,1), result(Bool)]
L1315: In this case, the sort check used by `seqstrict` and by the `heat` and `cool` attributes will be `isBool` instead of `isKResult`. This particular example does not really require use of the `result` attribute, but if the user wishes to evaluate a term of sort KResult further, the result attribute would be required.
L1316: ### `hybrid` attribute
L1317: 
L1318: In certain situations, it is desirable to treat a particular production which has the `strict` attribute as a result if the term has had its arguments fully evaluated. This can be accomplished by means of the `hybrid` attribute:
L1319: 
L1320:     k
L1321: 
L1322:     syntax KResult ::= Bool
L1323: 
L1324:     syntax BExp ::= Bool
L1325:                   | BExp "||" BExp [strict(1), hybrid]
L1326: 
L1327: This attribute is equivalent in this case to the following additional axiom being added to the definition of `isKResult`:
L1328: 
L1329:     k
L1330:     rule isKResult(BE1:BExp || BE2:BExp) => true requires isKResult(BE1)
L1331: 
L1332: Sometimes you wish to declare a production hybrid with respect to a predicate other than `isKResult`. You can do this by specifying a sort as the body of the `hybrid` attribute, e.g.:
L1333: 
L1334:     k
L1335: 
L1336:     syntax BExp ::= BExp "||" BExp [strict(1), hybrid(Foo)]
L1337: 
L1338: generates the rule:
L1339: 
L1340:     k
L1341: 
L1342:     rule isFoo(BE1:BExp || BE2:BExp) => true requires isFoo(BE1)
L1343: Properly speaking, `hybrid` takes an optional comma-separated list of sort names. If the list is empty, the attribute is equivalent to `hybrid(KResult)`. Otherwise, it generates hybrid predicates for exactly the sorts named.
L1344: ### Context aliases
L1345: 
L1346: Sometimes it is necessary to define a fairly complicated evaluation strategy for a lot of different operators. In this case, the user could simply write a number of complex `context` declarations, however, this quickly becomes tedious. For this purpose, K has a concept called a context alias. A context alias is a bit like a template for describing contexts. The template can then be instantiated against particular productions using the `strict` and `seqstrict` attributes.
L1347: Here is a (simplified) example taken from the K semantics of C++:
L1348: 
L1349:     k
L1350: 
L1351:     context alias [c]: <k> HERE:K ... </k> <evaluate> false </evaluate>
L1352:     context alias [c]: <k> HERE:K ... </k> <evaluate> true </evaluate> [result(ExecResult)]
L1353: 
L1354:     syntax Expr ::= Expr "=" Init [strict(c; 1)]
L1355: 
L1356: This defines the evaluation strategy during the translation phase of a C++ program for the assignment operator. It is equivalent to writing the following context declarations:
L1357: 
L1358:     k
L1359:     context <k> HOLE:Expr = I:Init ... </k> <evaluate> false </evaluate>
L1360:     context <k> HOLE:Expr = I:Init ... </k> <evaluate> true </evaluate> [result(ExecResult)]
L1361: 
L1362: What this is saying is, if the `evaluate` cell is false, evaluate the term like normal to a `KResult`. But if the `evaluate` cell is true, instead evaluate it to the `ExecResult` sort.
L1363: Essentially, we have given a name to this evaluation strategy in the form of the rule label on the context alias sentences (in this case, `c`). We can then say that we want to use this evaluation strategy to evaluate particular arguments of particular productions by referring to it by name in a `strict` attribute. For example, `strict(c)` will instantiate these contexts once for each argument of the production, whereas `strict(c; 1)` will instantiate it only for the first argument.
L1364: The special variable `HERE` is used to tell the compiler where you want to place the production that is to be heated or cooled.
L1365: You can also specify multiple context aliases for different parts of a production, for example:
L1366: 
L1367:     k
L1368: 
L1369:     syntax Exp ::= foo(Exp, Exp) [strict(left; 1; right; 2)]
L1370: 
L1371: This says that we can evaluate the left and right arguments in either order, but to evaluate the left using the `left` context alias and the right using the `right` context alias.
L1372: We can also say `seqstrict(left; 1; right; 2)`, in which case we additionally must evaluate the left argument before the right argument. Note, all strict positions are considered collectively when determining the evaluation order of `seqstrict` or the `hybrid` predicates.
L1373: 
L1374: A `strict` attribute with no rule label associated with it is equivalent to a `strict` attribute given with the following context alias:
L1375: 
L1376:     k
L1377: 
L1378:     context alias [default]: <k> HERE:K ... </k>
L1379: One syntactic convenience that is provided is that if you wish to declare the following context:
L1380: 
L1381:     k
L1382: 
L1383:     context foo(HOLE => bar(HOLE))
L1384: 
L1385: you can simply write the following:
L1386: 
L1387:     k
L1388: 
L1389:     syntax Foo ::= foo(Bar) [strict(alias)]
L1390: 
L1391:     context alias [alias]: HERE [context(bar)]
L1392: ## Pattern Matching
L1393: ### As Patterns
L1394: 
L1395: New syntax has been added to K for matching a pattern and binding the resulting match in its entirety to a variable.
L1396: 
L1397: The syntax is:
L1398: 
L1399:     Pattern #as V::Var
L1400: 
L1401: In this case, Pattern, including any variables, is matched and the resulting variables are added to the substitution if matching succeeds. Furthermore, the term matched by Pattern is added to the substitution as V.
L1402: This code can also be used outside of any rewrite, in which case matching occurs as if it appeared on the left hand side, and the right hand side becomes a variable corresponding to the alias.
L1403: 
L1404: It is an error to use an as pattern on the right hand side of a rule.
L1405: ### Record-like KApply Patterns
L1406: 
L1407: We have added a syntax for matching on KApply terms which mimics the record syntax in functional languages. This allows us to more easily express patterns involving a KApply term in which we don't care about some or most of the children, without introducing a dependency into the code on the number of arguments which could be changed by a future refactoring.
L1408: 
L1409: The syntax is:
L1410: 
L1411:     record(... field1: Pattern1, field2: Pattern2)
L1412: Note that this only applies to productions that are prefix productions. A prefix production is considered by the implementation to be any production whose production items match the following regular expression:
L1413: 
L1414:     (Terminal(_)*) Terminal("(")
L1415:     (NonTerminal (Terminal(",") NonTerminal)* )?
L1416:     Terminal(")")
L1417: 
L1418: In other words, any sequence of terminals followed by an open parenthesis, an optional comma separated list of non-terminals, and a close parenthesis.
L1419: If a prefix production has no named nonterminals, a `record(...)` syntax is allowed, but in order to reference specific fields, it is necessary to give one or more of the non-terminals in the production names.
L1420: Note: because the implementation currently creates one production per possible set of fields to match on, and because all possible permutations of all possible subsets of a list of n elements is a number that scales factorially and reaches over 100 thousand productions at n=8, we currently do not allow fields to be matched in any order like a true record, but only in the same order as appears in the production itself.
L1421: Given that this only reduces the number of productions to the size of the power set, this will still explode the parsing time if we create large productions of 10 or more fields that all have names. This is something that should probably be improved, however, productions with that large of an arity are rare, and thus it has not been viewed as a priority.
L1422: ### Or Patterns
L1423: 
L1424: Sometimes you wish to express that a rule should match if one out of multiple patterns should match the same subterm. We can now express this in K by means of using the `#Or` ML connective on the left hand side of a rule.
L1425: 
L1426: For example:
L1427: 
L1428:     k
L1429: 
L1430:     rule foo #Or bar #Or baz => qux
L1431: 
L1432: Here any of foo, bar, or baz will match this rule. Note that the behavior is ill-defined if it is not the case that all the clauses of the or have the same bound variables.
L1433: ### Matching global context in function rules
L1434: 
L1435: On occasion it is highly desirable to be able to look up information from the global configuration and match against it when evaluating a function. For this purpose, we introduce a new syntax for function rules.
L1436: 
L1437: This syntax allows the user to match on function context from within a function rule:
L1438: 
L1439:     k
L1440: 
L1441:     syntax Int ::= foo(Int) [function]
L1442: 
L1443:     rule [[ foo(0) => I ]]
L1444:          <bar> I </bar>
L1445: 
L1446:     rule something => foo(0)
L1447: This is completely desugared by the K frontend and does not require any special support in the backend. It is an error to have a rewrite inside function context, as we do not currently support propagating such changes back into the global configuration. It is also an error if the context is not at the top level of a rule body.
L1448: 
L1449: Desugared code:
L1450: 
L1451:     k
L1452: 
L1453:     syntax Int ::= foo(Int, GeneratedTopCell) [function]
L1454:     rule foo(0, <generatedTop>
L1455:                   <bar> I </bar>
L1456:                   ...
L1457:                 </generatedTop> #as Configuration) => I
L1458:     rule <generatedTop>
L1459:            <k> something ... </k>
L1460:            ...
L1461:          </generatedTop> #as Configuration
L1462:       => <generatedTop>
L1463:            <k> foo(0, Configuration> ... </k>
L1464:            ...
L1465:          </generatedTop>
L1466: ### Collection patterns
L1467: 
L1468: It is allowed to write patterns on the left hand side of rules which refer to complex terms of sort Map, List, and Set, despite these patterns ostensibly breaking the rule that terms which are functions should not appear on the left hand side of rules. Such terms are destructured into pattern matching operations.
L1469: 
L1470: The following forms are allowed:
L1471:     // 0 or more elements followed by 0 or 1 variables of sort List followed by
L1472:     // 0 or more elements
L1473:     ListItem(E1) ListItem(E2) L:List ListItem(E3) ListItem(E4)
L1474: 
L1475:     // the empty list
L1476:     .List
L1477: 
L1478:     // 1 or more list update operations applied to a variable
L1479:     L:List [ K1 <- E1 ] [ K2 <- E2 ]
L1480: 
L1481:     // 0 or more elements in any order plus 0 or 1 variables of sort Set
L1482:     // in any order
L1483:     SetItem(K1) SetItem(K2) S::Set SetItem(K3) SetItem(K4)
L1484: 
L1485:     // the empty set
L1486:     .Set
L1487:     // 0 or more elements in any order plus by 0 or 1 variables of sort Map
L1488:     // in any order
L1489:     K1 |-> E1 K2 |-> E2 M::Map K3 |-> E3 K4 |-> E4

L1491:     // the empty map
L1492:     .Map

L1494: Here K1, K2, K3, K4 etc can be any pattern except a pattern containing both function symbols and unbound variables. An unbound variable is a variable whose binding cannot be determined by means of decomposing non-set-or-map patterns or map elements whose keys contain no unbound variables.

L1498: 
L1499: In the above examples, E1, E2, E3, and E4 can be any pattern that is normally allowed on the lhs of a rule.
L1500: When a map, set, or list key contains function symbols, we know that the variables in that key are bound (because of the above restriction), so it is possible to evaluate the function to a concrete term prior to performing the lookup.
L1501: 
L1502: Indeed, this is the precise semantics which occurs; the function is evaluated and the result is looked up in the collection.
L1503: 
L1504: For example:
L1505: 
L1506:     k
L1507:     syntax Int ::= f(Int) [function]
L1508:     rule f(I:Int) => I +Int 1
L1509:     rule <k> I:Int => . ... </k> <state> ... SetItem(f(I)) ... </state>
L1510: 
L1511: This will rewrite `I` to `.` if and only if the state cell contains `I +Int 1`.
L1512: 
L1513: Note that in the case of Set and Map, one guarantee is that K1, K2, K3, and K4 represent /distinct/ elements. Pattern matching fails if the correct number of distinct elements cannot be found.
L1514: ### Matching on cell fragments
L1515: 
L1516: K allows matching fragments of the configuration and using them to construct terms and use as function parameters.
L1517: 
L1518:     k
L1519: 
L1520:     configuration <t>
L1521:                     <k> #init ~> #collectOdd ~> $PGM </k>
L1522:                     <fs>
L1523:                       <f multiplicity="*" type="Set"> 1 </f>
L1524:                     </fs>
L1525:                   </t>
L1526: The `#collectOdd` construct grabs the entire content of the `<fs>` cell. We may also match on only a portion of its content. Note that the fragment must be wrapped in a `<f>` cell at the call site.
L1527: 
L1528:     k
L1529: 
L1530:     syntax KItem ::= "#collectOdd"
L1531:     rule <k> #collectOdd => collectOdd(<fs> Fs </fs>) ... </k>
L1532:          <fs> Fs </fs>
L1533: 
L1534: The `collectOdd` function collects the items it needs
L1535: 
L1536:     k
L1537:     syntax Set ::= collectOdd(FsCell) [function]
L1538:     rule collectOdd(<fs> <f> I </f> REST </fs>) => SetItem(I) collectOdd(<fs> REST </fs>) requires I %Int 2 ==Int 1
L1539:     rule collectOdd(<fs> <f> I </f> REST </fs>) =>            collectOdd(<fs> REST </fs>) requires I %Int 2 ==Int 0
L1540:     rule collectOdd(<fs> .Bag </fs>) => .Set
L1541: ### `all-path` and `one-path` attributes to distinguish reachability claims
L1542: 
L1543: As the Haskell backend can handle both one-path and all-path reachability claims, but both these are encoded as rewrite rules in K, these attributes can be used to clarify what kind of claim a rule is.
L1544: In addition of being able to annotate a rule with one of them (if annotating with more at the same time, only one of them would be chosen), one can also annotate whole modules, to give a default claim type for all rules in that module.
L1545: 
L1546: Additionally, the Haskell backend introduces an extra command line option for the K frontend, `--default-claim-type`, with possible values `all-path` and `one-path` to allow choosing a default type for all claims.
L1547: ### Set Variables
L1548: #### Motivation
L1549: 
L1550: Set variables were introduced as part of Matching Mu Logic, the mathematical foundations for K. In Matching Mu Logic, terms evaluate to sets of values. This is useful for both capturing partiality (as in `3/0`) and capturing non-determinism (as in `3 #Or 5`). Consequently, symbol interpretation is extended to have a collective interpretation over sets of input values.
L1551: Usually, K rules are given using regular variables, which expect that the term they match is both defined and has a unique interpretation.
L1552: 
L1553: However, it is sometimes useful to have simplification rules which work over any kind of pattern, be it undefined or non-deterministic. This behavior can be achieved by using set variables to stand for any kind of pattern.
L1554: #### Syntax
L1555: 
L1556: Any variable prefixed by `@` will be considered a set variable.
L1557: #### Example
L1558: 
L1559: Below is a simplification rule which motivated this extension:
L1560: 
L1561:       rule #Ceil(@I1:Int /Int @I2:Int) =>
L1562:         {(@I2 =/=Int 0) #Equals true} #And #Ceil(@I1) #And #Ceil(@I2)
L1563:         [anywhere]
L1564: 
L1565: This rule basically says that `@I1:Int /Int @I2:Int` is defined if `@I1` and `@I2` are defined and `@I2` is not 0. Using sets variables here is important as it allows the simplification rule to apply any symbolic patterns, without caring whether they are defined or not.
L1566: This allows simplifying the expression `#Ceil((A:Int /Int B:Int) / C:Int)` to:
L1567: 
L1568:     {(C =/=Int 0) #Equals true} #And #Ceil(C) #And ({(B =/=Int 0) #Equals true}
L1569:     #And #Ceil(B) #And #Ceil(A)`
L1570: 
L1571: See cite120†kframework/kore#729†github.com for more details.
L1572: #### SMT Translation
L1573: 
L1574: K makes queries to an SMT solver (Z3) to discharge proof obligations when doing symbolic execution. You can control how these queries are made using the attributes `smtlib`, `smt-hook`, and `smt-lemma` on declared productions. These attributes guide the prover when it tries to apply rules to discharge a proof obligation.
L1575:   * `smt-hook(...)` allows you to specify a term in SMTLIB2 format which should be used to encode that production, and assumes that all symbols appearing in the term are already declared by the SMT solver.
L1576:   * `smtlib(...)` allows you to declare a new SMT symbol to be used when that production is sent to Z3, and gives it uninterpreted function semantics.
L1577:   * `smt-lemma` can be applied to a rule to encode it as a conditional equality when sending queries to Z3. A rule `rule LHS => RHS requires REQ` will be encoded as the conditional equality `(=> REQ (= (LHS RHS))`. Every symbol present in the rule must have an `smt-hook(...)` or `smtlib(...)` attribute.
L1578:     k
L1579: 
L1580:     syntax Int ::= "~Int" Int          [function, klabel(~Int_), symbol,
L1581:                                         smtlib(notInt)]
L1582:                  | Int "^%Int" Int Int [function, klabel(_^%Int__), symbol,
L1583:                                         smt-hook((mod (^ #1 #2) #3))]
L1584: 
L1585: In the example above, we declare two productions `~Int_` and `_^%Int__`, and tell the SMT solver to:
L1586:   * use uninterpreted function semantics for `~Int_` via SMTLIB2 symbol `notInt`, and
L1587:   * use the SMTLIB2 term `(mod (^ #1 #2) #3)` (where `#N` marks the `N `th production non-terminal argument positions) for `_^%Int__`, where `mod` and `^` already are declared by the SMT solver.
L1588: #### Caution
L1589: 
L1590: Set variables are currently only supported by the Haskell backend. The use of rules with set variables should be sound for all other backends which just execute by rewriting, however it might not be safe for backends which want to guarantee coverage.
L1591: 
L1592: ### Variables occurring only in the RHS of a rule
L1593: 
L1594: This section presents possible scenarios requiring variables to only appear in the RHS of a rule.
L1595: #### Summary
L1596: 
L1597: Except for `?` variables and `!` (fresh) variables, which are required to only appear in the RHS of a rule, all other variables must also appear in the LHS of a rule. This restriction also applies to anonymous variables; in particular, for claims, `?_` (not `_`) should be used in the RHS to indicate that something changes but we don't care to what value.
L1598: To support specifying random-like behavior, the above restriction can be relaxed by annotating a rule with the `unboundVariables` attribute whenever the rule intentionally contains regular variables only occurring in the RHS.
L1599: #### Introduction
L1600: 
L1601: K uses question mark variables of the form `?X` to refer to existential variables, and uses `ensures` to specify logical constraints on those variables. These variables are only allowed to appear in the RHS of a K rule.
L1602: 
L1603: If the rules represent rewrite (semantic) steps or verification claims, then the `?` variables are existentially quantified at the top of the RHS; otherwise, if they represent equations, the `?` variables are quantified at the top of the entire rule.
L1604: Note that when both `?`-variables and regular variables are present, regular variables are (implicitly) universally quantified on top of the rule (already containing the existential quantifications). This essentially makes all `?` variables depend on all regular variables.
L1605: 
L1606: All examples below are intended more for program verification / symbolic execution, and thus concrete implementations might choose to ignore them altogether or to provide ad-hoc implementations for them.
L1607: #### Example: Verification claims
L1608: 
L1609: Consider the following definition of a (transition) system:
L1610: 
L1611:     k
L1612: 
L1613:     module A
L1614:       rule foo => true
L1615:       rule bar => true
L1616:       rule bar => false
L1617:     endmodule
L1618: 
L1619: Consider also, the following specification of claims about the definition above:
L1620: 
L1621:     k
L1622: 
L1623:     module A-SPEC
L1624:       rule [s1]: foo => ?X:Bool
L1625:       rule [s2]: foo =>  X:Bool  [unboundVariables(X)]
L1626:       rule [s3]: bar => ?X:Bool
L1627:       rule [s4]: bar =>  X:Bool  [unboundVariables(X)]
L1628:     endmodule
L1629: ##### One-path interpretation
L1630:   * (s1) says that there exists a path from `foo` to some boolean, which is satisfied easily using the `foo => true` rule
L1631:   * (s3) says the same thing about `bar` and can be satisfied by either of `bar => true` and `bar => false` rules
L1632:   * (s2) and (s4) can be better understood by replacing them with instances for each element of type `Bool`, which can be interpreted that both `true` and `false` are reachable from `foo` for (s2), or `bar` for (s4), respectively.
L1633:     * (s2) cannot be verified as we cannot find a path from `foo` to `false`.
L1634:     * (s4) can be verified by using `bar => true` to show `true` is reachable and `bar => false` to achieve the same thing for `false`
L1635: ##### All-path interpretation
L1636: 
L1637:   * (s1) says that all paths from `foo` will reach some boolean, which is satisfied by the `foo => true` rule and the lack of other rules for `foo`
L1638: 
L1639:   * (s3) says the same thing about `bar` and can be satisfied by checking that both `bar => true` and `bar => false` end in a boolean, and there are no other rules for `bar`
L1640:   * (s2) and (s4) can be better understood by replacing them with instances for each element of type `Bool`, which can be interpreted that both `true` and `false` are reachable in all paths originating in `foo` for (s2), or `bar` for (s4), respectively. This is a very strong claim, requiring that all paths originating in `foo` (`bar`) pass through both `true` and `false`, so neither (s2) nor (s4) can be verified.
L1641: 
L1642: Interestingly enough, adding a rule like `false => true` would make both (s2) and (s4) hold.
L1643: #### Example: Random Number Construct `rand()`
L1644: 
L1645: The random number construct `rand()` is a language construct which could be easily conceived to be part of the syntax of a programming language:
L1646: 
L1647:     k
L1648: 
L1649:     Exp ::= "rand" "(" ")"
L1650: 
L1651: The intended semantics of `rand()` is that it can rewrite to any integer in a single step. This could be expressed as the following following infinitely many rules.
L1652: 
L1653:     k
L1654:     rule  rand() => 0
L1655:     rule  rand() => 1
L1656:     rule  rand() => 2
L1657:       ...    ...
L1658:     rule rand() => (-1)
L1659:     rule rand() => (-2)
L1660:       ...    ...
L1661:
